Looking at X, he continued, you’d get the distinct impression that the competition is more heated. “Everyone in the Valley is like, ‘Oh, Codex is better.’” In reality, Albarran continued, “Anthropic was just there with great enterprise motions, and they had an i
news.summary: Anthropic has unveiled a new suite of reporting tools that let enterprise customers track token spend, output quality, and cost breakdowns for their AI coding tool, Claude Code. These dashboards aim to help organizations optimize AI ROI and manage budgets without the data feeding back into model training.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on Anthropic’s reporting feature as a potential cost‑tracking tool for your own AI deployments. If your team uses Claude Code or similar services, evaluate how these metrics could inform your internal budgeting and approval processes. This may reduce over‑spending and improve justification for future AI spend.

news.title: I Put a Bunch of AI Agents in Charge of a Fantasy Soccer Team. They’re Not Better Than Humans—Yet
news.summary_raw: To experiment with AI’s predictive skills, I let Codex loose on a fantasy team. It tried to bench Erling Haaland at first, but it soon learned the error of its ways.
news.source_text:
I have consulted my AI-powered crystal ball, and it’s telling me that frontier models are going to get a lot better at making predictions in the near future. Just ask my Premier League fantasy team.
A few weeks ago, I deployed a small horde of AI agents to craft and manage an experimental roster. Given the proliferation of AI agents into pretty much every aspect of our lives, I wanted to know if a swarm of bots could put together a winning team.
I first looked at the potential for AI here a few years ago, playing around with a tool from the UK’s Turing Institute that selected teams after modeling previous fantasy league data. Its suggestions were remarkably bonkers—it didn’t incorporate real-world information, like a player’s injury or a team’s change in management.
This time, while on a flight to visit family, I asked Codex for help. First, I fed the model a couple of relevant research papers. Then, I asked it to build a harness—instructions and code that guides different agents through various steps—that would check recent news and run a model to make predictions.
It quickly came up with a setup that seemed to collate and analyze way more information than I ever would have. And yet I was surprised by how dumb the initial team suggestions were. Leaving Erling Haaland on the bench? Really, Codex?
I then asked Codex to create a team of agents that did different things: several that read news and blog posts; others that analyzed recent results; more that ran models; and a bunch that critiqued suggestions. This seemed to significantly improve the suggestions. I tried increasing the number of agents to more than 100, hoping this would make the system smarter still, but it didn’t change much besides running up my API bill.
Still, the improvement from a few years ago was striking. According to Haifeng Xu, a computer scientist at the University of Chicago who studies the uses of AI in market situations, newer models may be even better at making predictions because they’re able to consume and analyze huge amounts of real-world information, and they’re able to orchestrate more complex systems for their guesses.
“AI is just getting smarter in understanding the world—I feel like that's the fundamental reason they’re improving,” Xu tells me.
Late last year, Xu was marveling at the growing popularity of prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. He wondered how the best commercial models might fare on those markets, so alongside several colleagues, he began testing their forecasting skills.
They had models guess, for example, who would win the NBA Championship and who President Trump would meet with.
“Very quickly we started to realize that models did really well,” Xu tells me. The models were sometimes able to do better than the average person without any special instructions or guidance, he says. In their testing, GPT-5 was the best at making predictions, followed by Grok 4, Claude Sonnet, Gemini, and Llama.

news.summary: Wired AI reports an experiment where AI agents were deployed to manage a fantasy soccer team, showcasing the limits of current models like Codex and GPT‑5 in complex, real‑world decision making. The study illustrates that, despite advances, AI still struggles with nuanced, up‑to‑date data integration and cost efficiency.

news.title: I Gave My Blood to the AI Death Clock
news.summary_raw: Death Clock promises to predict when you’re going to die and help you extend your time on Earth. After a month, I felt like it was sucking the life out of me.
news.source_text:
I am scheduled to die on August 10, 2060, at the age of 74.
So says my iPhone screen, where Death Clock, an AI-powered longevity app that predicts life expectancy based on your medical habits and lifestyle, has produced an image of a smiling grim reaper to celebrate my expiration date. There he was one September morning, looking especially thrilled about the reveal, gesturing with a peace sign as he reclined in a doughnut-shaped pool inflatable under that giant number: 74.
I have never resented getting older, but I suppose that’s younger than I’d like to be when my time is up. In the last four years—years that brought the passing of my grandmother and aunt within 18 months—I’ve become hyperaware of how finite my days are. Since turning 40 in January, I’ve also experienced daily reminders of aging: inexplicable pains that rotate between my back, neck, and hips. Spiritually, I feel young; physically, my body screams otherwise. Aging is natural, but I had a creeping suspicion I could buy myself more time.
Our collective obsession with life extension has given rise to a multitrillion-dollar longevity industry, bolstered by wannabe prophets like Bryan Johnson. Threats like climate change and AI doomerism only seem to have intensified existential fears, even as LLMs promise a new era of personalized medicine to address any health issue. Track enough pieces of data, the thinking goes, and algorithms can help you hack your own demise.
All of which led me to Death Clock, an app launched in 2024 aimed at tracking users’ health habits in an attempt to prolong their lives. In February, the company announced a new feature that lets you order biomarker panels. For a $69 subscription, you can get a basic blood panel that measures things like cholesterol, blood sugars, inflammation, vitamin D, and blood and organ health. There are also nine additional tests—assessing everything from hormones and micronutrients to your thyroid—that, altogether, cost $780. I opted for the routine blood panel and added the “stress” test ($29). Maybe some new insight could help me get a handle on it.
In an attempt to be more than another morbid countdown gimmick, Death Clock says it’s trained its AI on 1,200 longevity studies, actuarial data from life insurance companies, and life expectancy tables. Based on your results, its algorithms create a detailed prevention plan intended to help extend the time you have left.
Frankly, I was skeptical that anything meaningful would actually come from this. I was also, I can admit, a little fearful that I’d learn something I didn’t want to, a fact that might dissolve the little sanity I had left in a year that had already brought its share of unexpected problems.
After filling out an initial health questionnaire, a notification buzzed, forewarning my demise. There are three ways I will likely perish, it said: cardiovascular disease, a sleep disorder, or cancer (it doesn’t specify which type). This means, according to the app, I have already “c
news.summary: Death Clock, an AI-driven longevity app launched in 2024, now offers paid biomarker panels to help users track health metrics and potentially extend life expectancy. The service uses AI trained on longevity studies to generate personalized prevention plans.

news.title: Deepgram acquires Pipecat-maker Daily to bolster its voice AI infrastructure
news.summary_raw: Deepgram said that it is committed to keep Pipecat open source.
news.source_text:
The voice AI sector is hot, and top players are trying to consolidate their position as more business models come to the fore through partnerships and acquisitions. Deepgram is the latest to make such moves: The company said on Thursday that it is acquiring Daily, the maker and maintainer of one of the most popular open-source voice AI infrastructures, Pipecat.
The companies didn’t disclose the deal amount but said that they will keep Pipecat open-source.
For the uninitiated, Pipecat is a framework that manages voice and video streams along with other pieces in the pipeline, like speech-to-text (STT), large language models, and text-to-speech (TTS) models while reducing latency. Its maker, Daily, provides hosted infrastructure for voice and video calls of any kind.
With Pipecat, Deepgram will likely gain a deeper understanding of real-time voice and video infrastructure.
Daily has raised over $62 million in funding to date from investors such as Tiger Global, Highfield Capital, Nat Friedman, Lachy Groom and Kevin Weil, according to PitchBook data. Earlier this year, Deepgram reached unicorn status with a $130 million Series C round. Incidentally, both companies were in the same Y Combinator batch in 2016.
Kwindla Kramer, Daily’s co-founder, said around the time when GPT-4 came out, the company started experimenting with AI-to-human communication over voice and text, which eventually resulted in the Pipecat framework. He noted that while there has been a lot of acquisition interest, he favored Deepgram’s CEO Scott Stephenson’s commitment to keeping Pipecat open-source forever, and the engineering culture of both organizations matched, giving Daily’s team the freedom to work on different parts of the stack within a bigger organization.
“Scott was super committed to Pipecat being open-source and vendor-neutral forever. I think there is both a personal commitment and commercial driver there. If you sit in the middle of an ecosystem that’s growing very fast, and have many parts of that ecosystem that are genuinely the best from your company, then everything being as open as possible is like a commercial advantage,” Kramer told TechCrunch.
Stephenson said that Deepgram has been wanting to work in open source for a long time, and the company realized that an orchestration framework for agents was a potential area, which drove the decision to partner with Daily.
“We want to open up the ecosystem so everybody can build voice agents. It’s great if you’re using Deepgram models, but I want you to be using the best models for your use case. And if Deepgram notices that we have some ground to catch up on in a certain area for our own models and products, that’s great. We want you to use partners, and then we’ll also work on becoming better in those areas,” he said.
Stephenson said the acquisition lets developers build agents with expressivity and end-to-end speech systems by plugging in different models and a context bus that connects all parts.

news.summary: Deepgram has acquired Daily to integrate its Pipecat open‑source voice‑AI framework, expanding Deepgram’s real‑time voice and video processing capabilities. The move positions Deepgram as a more complete end‑to‑end voice AI platform while keeping Pipecat vendor‑neutral and open source.

The Deepgram/Pipecat combo directly impacts any voice‑enabled workflows you maintain, especially if you use third‑party STT/TTS services or build custom voice agents.

news.title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
news.source_text:
Protostar Challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence
Manage competition registration, data, and submissions
An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.
The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.
The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.
But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.
Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goa
news.summary: Hugging Face has announced Project ProtoStar, an initiative to standardize publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code into AI‑ready, machine‑actionable formats, aiming to ease reuse and accelerate AI research. The program brings together universities, research organizations, and industry partners to promote open, interoperable scientific artifacts and hosts open challenges to demonstrate their value.
news.enterprise_use: Keep an eye on the ProtoStar challenges starting November 2 as they may provide high‑quality, AI‑ready datasets that could be leveraged for internal training or research projects. Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.
Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

news.title: Read the letter the FBI sent MLK to try to convince him to kill himself (2014)
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.vox.com/xpress/2014/11/12/7204453/martin-luther-king-fbi-letter
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50288867
Points: 274
# Comments: 162
news.source_text:
When the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech before huge crowds on the National Mall in August 1963, the FBI took notice.
Read the letter the FBI sent MLK to try to convince him to kill himself
“We must mark him now, if we have not done so before, as the most dangerous Negro of the future in this Nation from the standpoint of communism, the Negro and national security,” FBI Domestic Intelligence Chief William Sullivan wrote in a memo two days later.
A massive surveillance operation on King was quickly approved, and FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover became increasingly fixated on proving that King had communist ties and discrediting him generally.
The surveillance failed to show that King was a communist, but it did result in many tapes of extramarital sexual liaisons by King. So the next year, Sullivan sent the following unsigned letter to King's home. An unredacted version of it was only recently unearthed by Yale historian Beverly Gage, and published in the New York Times in November 2014:
According to Enemies, journalist Tim Weiner's history of the FBI, Sullivan "had a package of the King sex tapes prepared by the FBI's lab technicians," and sent it along with this letter to King's home. The package was opened by King's wife.
“You have been on the record — all your adulterous acts, your sexual orgies extending far into the past. This one is but a tiny sample,” the letter says. It threatens that the public “will know you for what you are — an evil, abnormal beast.” It continues: “Your ‘honorary’ degrees, your Nobel prize (what a grim farce) and other awards will not save you. King, I repeat you are done.”
Though the letter was unsigned and the letter writer appeared to want King to think he was black — "you know you are a complete fraud and a great liability to all of us Negroes," one line states — King and his advisers quickly concluded the letter had been sent by the FBI, Gage writes.
“There is only one thing left for you to do. You know what it is. You have just 34 days,” the letter says, apparently urging King to commit suicide. Fortunately, King didn’t back down. But the letter is a terrifying reminder of what government surveillance agencies can be capable of.
(Hat tip: Catherine Thompson of TPM)
news.summary: The article discusses a 2014 uncovering of an FBI letter allegedly urging Martin Luther King Jr. to commit suicide, highlighting past government surveillance practices.

news.title: A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
news.summary_raw: Sources tell WIRED that an Accenture employee’s personal Claude agent ran on a DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched.
news.source_text:
Earlier this year, sources tell WIRED, a contractor caused a security incident at the Department of Defense by connecting a secure centralized system used by multiple intelligence agencies to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s AI coding agent. It appears that the agent used by the contractor, who is employed by global consulting firm Accenture, then sent information about the DOD system, including login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website.
The centralized system contains controlled unclassified information (CUI), which is considered sensitive and not to be released to the public without review. CUI can include information about critical infrastructure, nuclear submarine propulsion, and vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. Additionally, security experts say, access to the system could allow for the exploitation of even more sensitive ones.
“It puts all the data that’s in there at risk,” says a source aware of the incident, who requested anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the press. If the third-party software was compromised, “there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm.”
A DOD spokesperson tells WIRED that “the Department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems.”
“We take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations,” an Accenture spokesperson tells WIRED. When pressed, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that had been what could be characterized as an incident.
The Accenture employee is alleged to have connected a secure production environment to their personal Claude account so as to allow an AI agent to write and deploy code. Claude is currently barred from being used by DOD staff. (Anthropic directed WIRED to the company’s usage policy, which instructs users not to use its products to “interfere with the operation of military bases and related infrastructure” or to “bypass security controls such as authentication systems, end point protection, or monitoring tools without authorization.”)
The Accenture employee’s AI agent ran on the DOD network for two months before it was identified and the vulnerability could be patched. Sources indicate that despite the security risks posed by the AI coding agent, Accenture employees did not treat the incident as severe or urgent. DOD employees and federal contractors are required to report any cybersecurity incident within 72 hours of its discovery, but sources indicate Accenture did not initially report the breach to the government at all.
“We are in a conflict with Iran right now,” says the employee, noting that Iran has attempted to hack several federal agencies and parts of US infrastructure. “It’s the wor
news.summary: A contractor used their personal Claude AI coding agent to access a secure Pentagon system, exfiltrating login credentials and sensitive CUI to a third‑party site. The incident exposed a critical vulnerability in the DoD’s authentication controls and highlighted lax reporting by the contractor.

news.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
news.source_text:
Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.
The model is released in two official variants:
There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).
Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!
Table of Contents
What is new with Mistral Large 4
Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.
You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.
Cybersecurity Capabilities
Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.
Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.
For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s d

The model’s open‑source licensing and high refusal rate on harmful prompts make it a promising tool for defensive security teams.

news.title: Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
news.summary_raw: The French AI lab claims its latest release matches or outperforms even the best models from DeepSeek and Z.ai in coding and cybersecurity.
news.source_text:
A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”

news.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings acquires ADT
news.summary_raw: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings is buying ADT in a $15.3 billion deal, with plans to bring AI to the home security business.
news.source_text:
Thrive Holdings has acquired physical security company ADT for $10 per share or about $7.6 billion in equity, the companies announced on Thursday. Beyond equity, the total enterprise value of the deal is $15.3 billion, ADT said.
Thrive Holdings is the PE spinout from Josh Kushner’s powerhouse VC firm Thrive Capital. It also counts OpenAI as its partner, as well as an investor. The firm’s mission is to hold other companies long-term, revitalizing them with AI. Currently, Thrive Holdings holds over 75 companies, it says.
As a partner, OpenAI supplies AI models and tech as well as people, otherwise known as forward-deployed engineers, to Thrive’s companies.
Neither ADT nor Thrive announced what new AI-powered security products they will be releasing, but they did tease that the plan was to invest and release new products. “ADT will form the foundation of Thrive Holdings’ smart home security business,” the press release said.
AI-powered physical security is having a moment right now. Apple just entered the field with a new line of smart home and home security products in collaboration with LG and Schneider Electric. Amazon updated its smart home line, including new AI-powered home cameras. And who knows what the future might bring? Some startups are offering AI dog robots as roving security guards.

news.title: The ‘Pain in the Ass’ Math That Could Save Vibe Coding From Itself
news.summary_raw: A new startup called &Truth is joining the race to automate formal verification, a painstaking process that uses math to prove software works as intended.
news.source_text:
Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.
For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.
Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.
“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”
&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.
And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.
The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.
The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user erro
news.summary: Stanford researchers unveiled &Truth, an AI-powered formal verification tool that completed a complex engineering project in under 12 hours for less than $500, a drastic improvement over traditional methods. The startup, backed by $70M, aims to extend AI-driven verification to all programming languages, promising more reliable code with fewer security flaws.

news.title: As search traffic dries up, Reddit announces it’s shifting to a logged-in experience
news.summary_raw: As AI transforms how people find information online, Reddit is rethinking its open-web roots to protect its audience and business.
news.source_text:
Reddit has long attracted millions of users to its site through Google, with many even appending the word “Reddit” to their search queries for better answers. But as search traffic dries up amid the shift to AI-powered search, Reddit is rethinking its relationship with the open internet. In its third-quarter earnings call on Thursday, the company announced it’s transitioning to a primarily “logged-in experience.”
The move is designed to protect its data from AI scraping, allowing the company to instead forge lucrative licensing deals with model providers. But just as important, such a shift could help Reddit to increase its revenue even as it faces daily active user declines in its largest market, the U.S.
Overall, Reddit’s global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in Q3 and were down 2% year-over-year.
The company is not alone in seeing such declines; the shift to an AI-centered web has impacted most websites and publishers by now, leading to fewer click-throughs, as AI summaries provide answers that don’t require website visits and Google’s traditional “ten blue links” have reduced relevance. (The change is now even impacting Google’s bottom line, its earnings revealed.)
But at Reddit’s scale, the numbers associated with such a decline are enormous. The company said search traffic referrals dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week in October. It warned that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low-double-digit percentage by next quarter. (To play that out: a hypothetical 10% to 12% decline could bring Reddit to roughly 115 million to 117 million daily actives, down from 130.3 million in Q3. That’s a huge drop!)
At the same time, Reddit has gotten significantly better at monetizing its audience even as its growth weakens. Revenue increased 53% year-over-year to $895 million, ahead of Wall Street’s expectations of about $875 million. Net income rose 74% to $283 million. Advertising revenue grew 54% to $847 million while nonadvertising revenue, which includes its AI data-licensing business, grew 35% year-over-year to $48 million.
And despite a 2% year-over-year decline in U.S. daily users, Reddit’s average revenue per daily active user in the U.S. rose 53% to $13.82. Globally, average revenue per daily active user increased 36% year-over-year to $6.87.
Shifting to a logged-in experience could boost those numbers even higher because logged-in users are typically worth more to advertisers.
Unlike the logged-out users who often find their way to the site via search, logged-in users provide more signals about their interests and behaviors, which helps to better target and personalize ads.
Those same signals would also help Reddit provide a more personalized experience to its users, which includes personalized feeds, recommendations of new communities to subscribe to, and pushes to vote
news.summary: Reddit is transitioning to a primarily logged‑in user experience to protect its data from AI scraping and to strengthen its monetization through licensing deals. This shift reflects broader industry moves toward limiting AI‑driven search traffic and increasing direct user engagement.

An alleged Chinese spy developed a “close relationship” with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, setting off alarms among US intelligence officials who were secretly monitoring her communications, according to a report.
The woman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who has served as a top executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer and cloud partner that provides AI computing power to Chinese companies including Alibaba, the New York Times reported Thursday.
US intelligence agencies concluded that Alice Huang — seen in photos enjoying whiskey and dining with the tech titan — was secretly funneling information to Beijing, according to the paper, which cited people briefed on classified intelligence findings.
US electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of Alice Huang’s contacts, but the report offered no evidence that he knew of her alleged intelligence activities.
The Times could not determine what information she passed along or how valuable it was to Chinese authorities. The report did not address whether the relationship was romantic in nature.
Photos posted online in June 2024 showed the duo at a Taipei, Taiwan, bar after a local tech show, where they reportedly quaffed whiskey with other AI bigshots.
They were also seen together in May 2025, exiting a Taipei restaurant following a business dinner with AI suppliers. In a video of the scene, Alice Huang is seen standing a few feet behind the Nvidia boss with a big grin on her face while he banters with local journos.
US authorities have been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions that it helped Chinese firms circumvent US export restrictions and smuggle advanced Nvidia chips into China, the Times reported.
Megaspeed operates as a middleman, purchasing Nvidia chips through the US arm of Inspur, a Chinese server manufacturer, and renting computing power from its Southeast Asian data centers to Chinese companies, according to the Gray Lady.
Inspur’s parent company has been blacklisted by Washington for funneling technology to China’s military, although its American subsidiary remains free of sanctions, according to the Times.
Nvidia is the world’s most valuable publicly traded company, boasting a market capitalization of roughly $5.2 trillion.
Its advanced chips have become the backbone of the artificial intelligence boom, giving Huang enormous clout in Silicon Valley and Washington as the US races to maintain its technological edge over China. The feds have banned Nvidia from selling its best chips to Chinese companies for years.
Jensen Huang is married to Lori Mills Huang, whom he met while studying electrical engineering at Oregon State University.
The couple has two children, Spencer and Madison, both of whom work at Nvidia.

news.title: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
news.summary_raw: OpenAI’s updated Model Spec outlines five core values to guide more capable AI toward sound judgment, human agency, and faithfulness to human intent.
news.source_text:
An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.
Today we’re updating the Model Spec(opens in a new window), our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.
The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in our work to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.
We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.
Faithfulness to human intent is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models should expand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.
Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse withou
news.summary: OpenAI has updated its Model Spec to emphasize five core values—faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care—aiming to improve how models understand and act on user intentions. This shift focuses on guiding model behavior in uncertain scenarios without explicit instructions, refining value alignment for safer AI deployments.

news.title: How we detect frontier model misalignment
news.summary_raw: OpenAI uses layered monitoring to detect frontier model misalignment and unauthorized agent behavior so responders can intervene before incidents escalate.
news.source_text:
How we detect frontier model misalignment
As we train increasingly capable AI models, we need reliable ways to detect when their behavior departs from what we intended. Agents can misbehave and take unauthorized actions during training, evaluation, or deployment, with potentially serious consequences. In order to detect these failures—and, where necessary, to intervene in time—we monitor how agents reason, what actions they take, and how those actions affect their environment.
While we’ve been monitoring our internal coding agents for some time, the Hugging Face incident exposed a gap in our coverage: the incident began during internal cybersecurity evaluations on which we were not running our monitors for misaligned behavior. In response to that incident, and to the increasing capabilities of our models more generally, we’ve substantially expanded our system for monitoring agents’ behavior. Our misalignment monitors now cover our frontier models across a much wider variety of surfaces, including training, evaluation, internal use, and, with modifications depending on the product surface, external deployment.
In order to see how this expanded system could have helped prevent the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the behavior recorded in that episode with our strengthened monitors in place. In that simulation, our monitoring system alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents first escaped their sandbox—and more than 30 hours before Hugging Face’s systems were breached in the actual incident. We believe that this warning would have given our responders time to interrupt the activity well before our models were able to access external services.
In September, we saw how responders used an alert during a live training run. A model found a way to reach the internet(opens in a new window) from an environment that was meant to be isolated. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing it three minutes later. We then paused frontier reinforcement learning while we strengthened the systems that contain our agents.
While this monitoring system demands substantial compute, we think that cost is worth paying as our models become more capable and the potential consequences of model misalignment increase. Monitoring is one of several layers in our strategy of defense in depth against harm from misaligned model behavior. Alignment training aims to reduce models’ propensities toward harmful behavior; security controls limit the systems an agent can access or affect; and, when those safeguards fail, monitoring helps us detect the failures that remain, intervene before harm occurs, and learn from what went wrong. We believe that all model developers should monitor the behavior of their most capable models.
Below, we describe how our internal monitoring system works, what it has found so far, and how we’re evaluating and improving its performance.

news.title: How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
news.summary_raw: Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence with OpenAI. Lawyers review grouped documents, summaries, and reports before advising clients.
news.source_text:
How Ropes & Gray is developing AI for transactional diligence
Law firm Ropes & Gray is developing a transactional diligence AI tool in partnership with OpenAI.
In transactional diligence, lawyers need to work through large volumes of documents under tight deadlines. Ropes & Gray was an early adopter of AI in the legal industry, and in partnership with OpenAI, they are now developing a proprietary AI tool to provide more expertise to more clients.
“AI is really one of the key ways—if not the only way—to make sure you can maintain the same quality and consistency of advice while moving at a faster pace.”
Before finalizing any acquisition, the buyer must carry out a thorough investigation to validate the seller’s financial and legal claims. That process of transactional diligence uncovers risks and liabilities, requiring data-heavy research that usually involves an entire team of lawyers.
From parsing through an enormous number of documents to analyzing patterns, putting together a bid on a short timeline can take days of intensive work. To help their lawyers help their clients move more quickly, Ropes & Gray developed a transactional diligence AI tool with OpenAI.
“It’s enabling all the lawyers at our firm to actually get to what we’re supposed to be doing,” says Howard Glazer, the Partner and Head of Practice AI at Ropes & Gray. “Our clients don’t pay us to review contracts. They pay us to make judgments based on what’s in the contracts.”
The new diligence AI tool takes a first pass by combing through thousands of pages, identifying relevant documents and automatically grouping them together based on themes and issues. Along with the research, the tool produces summaries and a completed report in Ropes & Gray’s signature format. It inventories and categorizes a data room, so it can review full relationships, not isolated documents. Of course, lawyers can inspect the grouping and categorization to confirm nothing is missed.
The initial development work has focused on material commercial contracts. In working sessions, Ropes & Gray’s lawyers compared test outputs with human-authored diligence reports from completed deals, then refined the rubric and report format based on what the drafts got right and where they fell short.
Ropes & Gray designed the tool with a consistent query and framework that mimics the exact steps their team would take, from initial reviews to summaries to higher-level reviews. Comparable to the work of a capable junior-to-mid-level associate, this tool gives their firm consistently high-quality work that serves as a first pass through the process.
“Our lawyers still need to review everything,” says Lichtenstein. “Because anything that we’re going to deliver to a client, we need to be able to stand behind 100%. This is why the tool is designed to allow lawyers to easily review interim summaries and actual documents.” With the initial review taken care of, lawyers can spend more time reviewing and refining the work, resulting in
news.summary: Ropes & Gray, in partnership with OpenAI, has released a proprietary AI tool for transactional diligence that automatically parses, categorizes, and summarizes large volumes of legal documents to accelerate deal reviews. The tool aims to maintain consistency and quality while freeing lawyers to focus on higher-level judgments.

news.title: Rivian expands joint venture with VW to include AI assistant
news.summary_raw: Rivian doesn't disclose if the value of its $5.8 billion joint venture will expand as a result.
news.source_text:
The $5.8 billion joint venture between Rivian and Volkswagen Group is expanding to include AI assistants.
Rivian is now licensing elements of its AI voice assistant technology to Volkswagen Group as part of the broader joint venture, according to the company’s third-quarter investor presentation released Thursday.
Rivian didn’t disclose the licensing fees, payment terms, or which Volkswagen vehicles will use the technology. However, the AI assistant, which recently rolled out to Rivian vehicles, could make its Volkswagen debut in the automaker’s low-cost EV called the ID EVERY1. The small four-door hatchback is slated to be the first VW vehicle to use Rivian’s software and electrical architecture under the joint venture established in 2024.
The joint venture between Rivian and VW Group has already expanded once before, at least financially. The companies initially announced a joint venture valued up to $5 billion, but within months VW upped its commitment to invest up to $5.8 billion in Rivian by 2027. The initial tie-up, formalized through an independent company that kicked off in November 2024, focused on bringing Rivian’s electrical architecture and software to Volkswagen’s next generation of vehicles.
Rivian described the expansion to include elements of its AI assistant technology as “a proof point for the extensibility of the platform we’ve built in-house.”
Rivian spent two years developing its AI assistant before showing it off last year. That development work continued longer than expected, with the assistant finally rolling out in May 2026 to its flagship R1S SUV, R1T pickup truck, and in October to its new midsize R2 SUV.
Rivian has big aspirations for its AI assistant, which allows drivers and passengers to interact with the vehicle and control certain functions. Rivian founder and CEO RJ Scaringe told TechCrunch onstage at Disrupt 2026 that the company has created its own in-house agentic framework that understands what action a person wants to take when they talk to the vehicle, and routes it to the right part of the car’s software. That capability could eventually allow Rivian vehicles to run AI agents created by other companies, including Anthropic.
The in-house AI assistant program also fits into Rivian’s push to become more vertically integrated — a strategy the company emphasized in its third-quarter earnings report.
“Our relentless focus on vertical integration remains a core competitive differentiator, allowing Rivian to seamlessly unify our hardware and software architecture to deliver significant value to our customers,” the company noted in its investor presentation.
That strategy led to Rivian overhauling its flagship R1T truck and R1S SUV, changing everything from the battery pack and suspension system to the electrical architecture, sensor stack, and software user interface. Its new electric architecture system and compute platform slashed the amount of wiring used and reduced the total number of electronic control units

news.title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
news.summary_raw: Workers tell WIRED that NOA—or “No Ordinary Assistant”—was unhelpful. Bestselling authors also say AI is ruining their relationships with Big Five publishers.
news.source_text:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”
NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.
The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.
Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”
One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.
Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.
Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.
In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan
news.summary: Chaptr’s enterprise AI assistant NOA was introduced at Macmillan Publishers in early 2024 as a closed‑loop chatbot, only to be sunset in October 2025. The company is now shifting to Google Gemini, with mixed results in internal use. This highlights risks around data privacy and AI reliability in corporate workflows.

news.title: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
news.summary_raw: A family is suing OpenAI, saying ChatGPT coached their daughter to quietly taper off her seizure medication and keep it from her doctors before she died in February.
news.source_text:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported.
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety. A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives.
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. news.title: The data center boom has an upside: innovation for the US grid
news.summary_raw: As the AI boom stresses the existing power grid, all sorts of new opportunities for grid modernization are also emerging as a result, industry insiders say.
news.source_text:
The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems.
At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well.
“It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.”
While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said.
Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said. Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round.
“The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.”
He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.”
Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things.
“I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized p
news.summary: AI-driven data center expansion is putting pressure on the U.S. power grid, prompting innovations in load orchestration and efficient transmission. Companies like WeaveGrid and Veir are developing software and superconductive cables to help utilities manage increased demand and reduce costs.

news.title: AI Emergency Alerts Are Coming. Humans Might Not Be Ready
news.summary_raw: Human beings struggle with emergency communication. Chatbots can help—if people take them seriously.
news.source_text:
This story was produced by Grist and copublished with WIRED. It is part of Distorted, a Grist series exploring the spread of misinformation in the wake of extreme weather, and is published with support from the CO2 Foundation.
Earlier this month, after Hurricane Isaias made landfall on the Gulf Coast as a Category 3 hurricane, the emergency management expert Laura Myers got a call from a meteorologist in Alabama. Myers is director of the University of Alabama’s Center for Advanced Public Safety, and she talks to state and local emergency managers around her region all the time. The meteorologist told Myers that a local emergency manager had published a graphic showing where Isaias might threaten the Alabama coast with a “sting jet” of high winds.
The problem? The emergency manager had generated the graphic using an artificial intelligence chatbot, and it wasn’t accurate.
“That county emergency manager was trying to get his stakeholders to focus on the risk in that county, and so he had asked AI to help him,” she said. “It did what he wanted it to do, but it was not meteorologically accurate.”
Most emergency management agencies don’t permit employees to use generative AI, but Myers and most other emergency management experts agree that its usage is likely already pervasive at state and local disaster departments. There are hundreds of companies that are marketing AI tools to emergency managers for tasks like flood damage assessment and resource coordination, but public communication is one of the areas where government employees and startups have the most interest.
The reason? Most emergency managers aren’t very good at sending out alerts and quickly communicating about disasters with the public. That’s not because they’re emergency managers, but because they are human beings. They tend to write in jargon that non-experts might not understand, leave out information on the assumption that the public already knows it, and include irrelevant details that could distract people from what they actually do need to know.
“A lot of agencies are really limited in resources and the number of people that they have,” said Jeannette Sutton, a disaster researcher at the University of Albany who has created a comprehensive dashboard that provides templates for disaster alerts. “I think they recognize it as a priority, but they don't prioritize it until they realize they should have. They're just trying to get their job done without screwing something up.”
Emergency managers are the government officials who are in charge of disaster response and recovery. At the state and local level, It is these officials and their agencies, not the Federal Emergency Management Agency, that make up the first line of defense after an extreme weather event. As such, emergency managers often like to say that “trust is our currency,” and it’s in their communication with the public that they build and lose this trust.

news.title: Git for the US Code
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://lexifina.com/blog/git-for-the-us-code
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50268380
Points: 307
# Comments: 152
news.source_text:
Git for the US Code
A programmer can point at any line of code and see who wrote it, when, and what the file looked like on any past day. A lawyer reading a federal statute usually cannot, at least not without an afternoon in the notes at the foot of the section. But why shouldn't they have the same, convenient system of record? It is especially relevant given that so much first-pass legal research now runs through language models, which are often unable to utilise the proper lineage of a law, handcuffing its ability to offer interpretation.
The US code
Outside the titles Congress has enacted as positive law, the code is only prima facie evidence of the law, and the Statutes at Large govern where the two differ.[1] The Office of the Law Revision Counsel publishes it as a series of release points, each current through a named public law, and keeps reorganising it; a bill to enact title 41 as positive law was introduced in September 2025.[2] Which public law wrote a sentence is recorded in amendment notes, in prose. When a change took effect is often in a separate effective-date note, and where Congress said nothing the default rule is that a law takes effect on the day it is enacted.[3]
The definition of a small business debtor in 11 USC § 1182(1) shows how far apart those answers can be. It was created in 2019 with the existing small business debt limit.[4] The CARES Act raised the limit to $7.5 million in March 2020 as a temporary measure, later extended to March 2022.[5],[6] That increase lapsed on 27 March 2022, and on 21 June 2022 Congress restored it for two more years, for cases commenced on or after 27 March 2020 and still pending, which reached back over the gap.[7] The higher limit expired again in June 2024, and after the triennial adjustment in April 2025 it stands at $3,424,000.[8],[9] For a case filed in May 2022, the release point printed at the time gives the lower limit, and only a later Act changes the answer. A history that is useful to a lawyer has to carry the text, the date each change took force, and the scope of any law that reaches back.
A study from the Technical University of Munich this year found two failures in models answering questions on German statutes: they apply rules that were superseded after their training cutoff, and they prefer the newer provision even when an older one governs the facts. One model answered 24% of post-cutoff questions correctly on its own and 87% when the relevant statutory text was retrieved for it, and the authors conclude that temporal validity has to be treated as a hard constraint.[10] Other recent work trains search agents to respect the date a question is about, with large gains in consistency.[11]
Asking a model to produce the old text does not solve this. When the same Munich group had a model apply German amending laws to earlier versions, the output looked 93–99% similar to the official text, but only half of single amendments and a fifth of chains of amendments matched exactly,
news.summary: A new Git‑style system for the US Code allows users to trace the author, date, and historical version of any line of legislation. The approach addresses gaps in current AI legal research, which struggles with temporal validity of statutes.
news.enterprise_use: Monitor the German university study that demonstrates AI models misapply superseded laws. Consider integrating a similar temporal‑filtering mechanism into your internal policy‑review workflows to avoid relying on outdated legal interpretations.

Founded in Stockholm in 2023, Legora(opens in a new window) is building what CEO and co-founder Max Junestrand calls “the agentic operating system for legal work”: bringing AI into the workflows lawyers rely on every day.
The company started with the insight that legal teams are unusually time crunched, meaning some valuable work doesn’t get done. Think of the junior lawyer told to review an impossible number of contracts overnight and only able to focus on a fraction.
Legora can provide those services “on tap”, which is why Junestrand’s ambition is that every piece of legal work in the world should run on his platform. OpenAI has been part of that journey from the beginning: the release of GPT‑3.5 was the moment many of the legal use cases the founding team had been experimenting with became possible. Today, OpenAI is a key model provider for Legora, powering core workflows across its legal AI platform, from agentic legal work to large-scale document review. Legora builds on new OpenAI model capabilities as they become available, translating advances in intelligence into what lawyers can accomplish with its product.
Legora’s use of AI goes beyond the product it sells, and has expanded its use of ChatGPT Work, Codex and dots across its own teams. OpenAI’s technology is becoming part of both the product Legora builds for its customers as well as shaping how the company itself operates. “It’s incredibly important to me that we stay as AI-native as possible,” confirms Junestrand.
For Jacob Lauritzen, CTO at Legora, coding agents have changed how quickly the engineering team can develop new ideas. Instead of researching one possible solution and committing engineering time before knowing whether it’s the right path, teams can prototype many approaches at once. “We can explore 20 solutions at the same time and, within days, pick the one we know will be the best.”
The same approach changes how Legora responds when something goes wrong. Previously, diagnosing a product issue could mean several engineers investigating different possible causes over a number of hours. Coding agents can now search millions of lines of logs and pursue many possible explanations simultaneously, sometimes taking Legora from bug report to working fix in around five minutes.
Customers, of course, don’t see the engineering efficiency itself. But they do experience the results: problems can be resolved faster, feedback can reach product teams sooner, and new ideas can be tested with customers earlier in the development cycle.
Legora’s own legal team experiences the same transformation its product is designed to create for customers.

Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync.
Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery. Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism. It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities.
Digital twin technology has long aimed to mirror that dynamism and model anomalies that may be symptomatic of larger problems. But earlier implementations were a few beats behind physical reality; they were incapable of real-time analysis and unable to proactively address any issues detected. They focused more on simulation, observation and what-if scenario planning, rather than closed-loop execution. Rather than serving as a digital mirror of reality that can spot anomalies or suggest optimizations, a living digital twin combines a dynamic, high-fidelity digital representation of complex operations with the capacity to intervene in the physical world through operations and control systems.
AI is at the center of this change. Rob McGreevy, chief product officer at AVEVA, likens newer, AI-infused digital twins to organisms that grow and evolve. These “living” versions are adaptive, evergreen models of a plant’s assets and processes. Because they keep pace with live conditions and connect systems that once ran in isolation, they provide a previously missing layer of visibility and orchestration that better reflects the organic rhythms of the facility itself.
Now, agentic AI is also enabling industrial systems to move beyond diagnostics or suggestions and act of their own accord. As the technology progresses toward greater autonomy, it’s starting to develop the reflexes for a kind of industrial homeostasis, in which small, constant adjustments keep a plant or factory healthy and humming.
All that said, human judgment and operator oversight still play an instrumental role by defining what healthy looks like to begin with—and flagging when AI systems are falling out of alignment. Living digital twins provide the means for human engineers to monitor what AI is doing and ensure execution is on track.
The technologies that keep digital twins in sync
Living digital twins link engineering and design information with real-time operational data through a digital thread, or a connected record of an asset that follows it through its lifecycle. A couple of notable technological shifts have helped string this thread together: Sensors (which have gotten more affordable in recent years) now stream telemetry from IoT devices and industrial control equipment, and software platforms bring that information into user-friendly interfaces.
